messages.author: d588a03e58ea7e7f
messages.subject: Logo for ggplot?
parts:
Has ggplot gotten big and diverse enough that it could benefit from a logo?

I can think of a few places where it would appear:

* The ggplot website (http://ggplot2.org/)
** in lieu of the splot on the side (http://ggplot2.org/images/splot.gif)
** as a favicon in the title bar
** in the on-line version of the documentation
* As the avatar on the ggplot blog (http://www.tumblr.com/blog/ggplot2)
instead of the default silhouette.
* In any ggplot2 vignettes that get written
* In the second edition of the ggplot2 book ;)

Does this seem like a worthwhile idea? If so, what characteristics
should it have or avoid?

I have an idea for a logo, but I'll wait until at least tomorrow to post
it to give anyone else a chance to chime in.


--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

messages.author: d588a03e58ea7e7f
messages.subject: Re: Logo for ggplot?
parts:
On 8/13/2012 3:01 PM, Hadley Wickham wrote:
>> Does this seem like a worthwhile idea? If so, what characteristics should it
>> have or avoid?
>
> Sure - the main characteristic of a logo is that I'd need to like it ;)

The most important requirements are always the hardest to quantify :)

I'll briefly lay out my criteria, how they influenced the final design,
and then show the design.

Criteria:

* algorithmic (can be generated from code, specifically R)
* leverage existing ggplot look/identity
* focused on on-line presentation

How the criteria influenced the design:

ggplot2 has a distinctive look to how it produces data graphics.
However, that is not so helpful for a logo. Further, what makes a good
data graphic and what makes a good logo or icon is not the same. So I
didn't try to make the logo using ggplot itself. However, grid does
offer enough control that it does make a reasonable medium. Also, since
ggplot uses grid, there is a familial relationship.

The useful iconographic graphical aspects of ggplot which are useful are
the icons on the (old) documentation site for the different geoms and
stats. These have the additional advantage of being rendered using grid
and so that can be leveraged.

For online applications, a square icon works best. That also makes using
the older documentation icons easier since they are already square.

Design:

I took the icon for facet_grid (what I though as a most distinctive
aspect of ggplot) as the base, and then inside each of the 4 squares,
used different icons: scale_grey, geom_point, geom_dotplot, and scale_size.

The design is in the github repo https://github.com/BrianDiggs/ggicon

Included there is a rendered PDF
(https://github.com/BrianDiggs/ggicon/blob/master/ggicon.pdf?raw=true),
SVG (https://raw.github.com/BrianDiggs/ggicon/master/ggicon.svg), and
PNG (64x64)
(https://github.com/BrianDiggs/ggicon/blob/master/ggicon64.png). I
automatically created a 16x16 PNG, but it didn't look that good so I
went back and drew it by hand and that is included as ggicon16Custom.png
in the repository.

Comments, criticisms, or proposed changes welcome either on-list or on
github.

> Hadley

>


--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

messages.author: 17652242ec236632
messages.subject: Re: Logo for ggplot?
parts:
Brian,

Thanks for suggesting a logo. I think its a great idea. Can I build upon your suggestions/criteria? I'd suggest that the logo:

1. Also look good on a t-shirt

2. Can appear in the bottom of the plot without looking like an outlier or a toner/color test

3. Be immediately identifiable with ggplot2

http://logos.wikia.com/wiki/Logopedia collects corporate logos. They all seem to go for simplicity/recognizability. I like your idea of having a logo that can be made with ggplot. I think we can push the abilities of ggplot2 very far. For example, here's a half decent rendition of the RStudio logo with just a few lines of code:

ggplot() +
 geom_point(aes(x = 1, y = 1), color = "blue", size = 50) +
 geom_point(aes(x = 1.0, y = 0.955), color = "deepskyblue", 
   alpha = 0.5, size = 30) +
 geom_point(aes(x = 1.0, y = 0.965), color = "deepskyblue", 
   alpha =  0.4, size = 35) +
 geom_point(aes(x = 1.0, y = 0.975), color = "deepskyblue", 
   alpha = 0.3, size = 40) + 
 geom_text(aes(x = 1, y = 1), label = "R", colour = "white", 
   size = 25) +
 geom_point(aes(x = 1.0, y = 1.02), color = "white", 
   alpha = 0.25, size = 40) + 
 geom_point(aes(x = 1.0, y = 1.03), color = "white", 
   alpha = 0.25, size = 35) + 
 geom_point(aes(x = 1.0, y = 1.04), color = "white", 
   alpha = 0.3, size = 30) +   
 coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.5, 1.5), ylim = c(0.5, 1.5))

Okay, maybe a quarter decent. Can we have something colorful and eye catching like so?

Garrett

On 8/17/2012 6:05 AM, Brandon Hurr wrote:
> One pull/suggestion submitted.

[The pull request was to change the shape of the dot plot in the lower
right from circles to squares.]

I understand not having all the points be circles; there are other
possibilities that deserve to be represented. I'm not sure that is the
one I'd change, though.

> I'm also thinking that perhaps instead of
> two scatterplots (upper and lower right) with opposite slopes you do a
> different sort of plot. Perhaps a density plot with two colors or B&W?

I was thinking of them as a scatterplot and a bubble plot, but you are
right; they are really quite similar. I've tried a version replacing the
upper right scatter plot with a density plot. Check out the with_density
branch of the repo (https://github.com/BrianDiggs/ggicon/tree/with_density)

> Are you specifically avoiding color? I'm cool with that (small icons need
> high contrast and large patterns).

It's not so much that I'm specifically avoiding color as that I'm not
quite sure what to do with color. I made a version where the upper left
gradient was colored (with_color branch,
https://github.com/BrianDiggs/ggicon/tree/with_color), but then I'm not
sure how else to use color. I could just make the dotplot and bubble
plot each a single, but different, color. If we go with a density plot,
then there could be two densities, each in a different color. I'm not
sure how much would get lost when going to smaller sizes.
> It's a great idea and well needed.
Thanks.

On 8/17/2012 9:00 AM, Garrett Grolemund wrote:
> Brian,
>
> Thanks for suggesting a logo. I think its a great idea. Can I build upon
> your suggestions/criteria?
Certainly.

> I'd suggest that the logo:
>
> 1. Also look good on a t-shirt

That's not something I'd thought of. For a t-shirt, there would need to
be enough detail; you wouldn't want to see pixelation. Having it be
renderable as a vector graphic would address this. But there would also
need to be enough interesting at that resolution (without making it
worthless at low resolutions).

> 2. Can appear in the bottom of the plot without looking like an outlier or
> a toner/color test

I wouldn't like it appearing on all my plots that I make with ggplot. I
think anything would be distracting from the conveyance of information
that is the reason I'm creating the plot in the first place.
> 3. Be immediately identifiable with ggplot2

Yes. I deliberately avoided putting an "R" anywhere in the logo because
that isn't the main point of ggplot (although a "gg" wouldn't be bad). I
was trying to pick geoms/stats/etc. that ggplot is known for and does
well/easily to be part of the representation.

messages.subject: Re: Logo for ggplot?
parts:
On iPhones you can have an icon for the low resolution screens that has less detail than you would use on higher resolution screens. I think that idea applies here: one icon, intended to be used as an icon in small physical sizes, which can't have too much detail but must be recognizable. Then a larger version, clearly recognizable as the same 'brand' could have more detail and go on t-shirts and all the other branded swag we can put on Cafe Press (coffee cups, embossed notebooks, infant onesies ;-) Both could be b/w or color. So 4 versions.

Just a thought (having recently spent more time thinking about logos that I really wished). Bryan

messages.author: d31339b95f6e694c
messages.subject: Re: Logo for ggplot?
parts:
Hello,

Thanks for getting the ball rolling on this. Let me add my opinion

On 2012-Aug-16, at 21:12 , Brian Diggs <dig...@ohsu.edu> wrote:
>
> I'll briefly lay out my criteria, how they influenced the final design, and then show the design.
>
> Criteria:
>
> * algorithmic (can be generated from code, specifically R)

While I agree this is nice, I don't think this should get in the way of good design. I would start with finding a good design and then check whether it can be recreated (possibly altered a bit) in R (it will be possible: everything is possible in R, right?).
> * leverage existing ggplot look/identity
agreed
> * focused on on-line presentation
I would not stop at that. T-shirt, mugs and the like were already mentioned. Print is another requirement (2nd edition of the ggplot book?)

> How the criteria influenced the design:
>
> ggplot2 has a distinctive look to how it produces data graphics. However, that is not so helpful for a logo. Further, what makes a good data graphic and what makes a good logo or icon is not the same. So I didn't try to make the logo using ggplot itself. However, grid does offer enough control that it does make a reasonable medium. Also, since ggplot uses grid, there is a familial relationship.

If you really want to do it with code, I would try to stick with ggplot. The point of doing it in code, IHMO, is to be a demonstration of the versatility of said code/package. In that sense, having to default to grid instead of ggplot looks like an admission of failure. I think you can probably recreate your logo using ggplot by altering the theme quite a bit (which should be made easier by the new theming system!).

> Design:
>
> I took the icon for facet_grid (what I though as a most distinctive aspect of ggplot) as the base, and then inside each of the 4 squares, used different icons: scale_grey, geom_point, geom_dotplot, and scale_size.

I agree that facet_grid is distinctive but I feel that the proposed design still looks more like an "illustration" than like a logo. Think of the difference between the graphic on the R homepage and the R logo. Of course the difference is not as strong in your design but it still feels the same. It lacks some clearly identifiable feature. Using the letters "gg" somewhere might help in this respect.
In any case, I think it lacks the single most identifiable feature of ggplot graphics: bring us the gray background! ;)

Of course its easy to criticise, it's harder to actually do something! So thanks very much for your efforts. When I am back in the lab in a couple of weeks, I'll try to come up with something that builds on your idea while trying to fulfil the additional criteria I laid out above and you'll let me know what you think.

Thanks again,

Jean-Olivier Irisson

I like the basic idea, but I think it needs some tweaking to come
together as a coherent whole. Some ideas:

* Instead of the strong black lines between each panel, why not
alternate the background colours between white and grey? That would
allude less to facet_grid, and more to theme_bw() vs theme_grey()

* I'd like to see some more colour

* I think the panels on the right need a bit of tweaking so they don't
form a triangle - that draws the eye away, and makes the right side
look very different to the left.
